Data Analytics Case Study · PostgreSQL · Python · Power BI

What 8,691 restaurants reveal about where Swiggy should grow next

A full analytics pipeline across 9 Indian metros — from a scraped, broken CSV to a stakeholder dashboard that answers one question: where is the market mature, where is it thin, and where does the money actually sit?

RoleAnalyst, National Strategy (framing) Scope9 cities · 8,691 restaurants StackPostgreSQL → Python → Power BI SnapshotSwiggy partners, Jan 2022
01 — THE PREMISE

One question, dressed as a strategy brief

Imagine you have just joined Swiggy's national strategy team. Leadership wants to know where to put next year's energy across the company's nine biggest metros. They don't want a chart dump — they want a decision: which markets are mature, which are underserved, where quality is strongest, and where the pricing opportunity hides.

That brief became the spine of this project. Everything downstream — the schema, the analysis, the dashboard — points back at it. I picked the multi-city Swiggy dataset deliberately: most junior portfolios analyse a single city's Zomato data that recruiters have seen a hundred times. A genuine nine-metro comparison is rarer and forces you to think in terms of markets, not rows.

Source & scope note The dataset is publicly available on Kaggle (Swiggy restaurants data). It captures only restaurants where Swiggy operates as a delivery partner, frozen at January 2022. So findings describe Swiggy's competitive footprint in each city — not the total restaurant universe. Stating that limitation up front is part of the analysis, not a footnote to hide.

Five stages, one source of truth

The whole project runs as a reproducible chain. Raw text in, decision out — with every transformation documented so a stranger could re-run it.

Tools matched to the job: PostgreSQL for cleaning & modelling, Python (pandas, scipy) for statistics, Power BI for the stakeholder dashboard.

03 — THE MESSY DATA PROBLEM

The first lesson cost me a day

I started cleaning in Excel. Power Query threw 738 parsing errors, the filter only showed 3 of 9 cities, and chunks of the file went blank past a few thousand rows. The culprit was textbook: web-scraped address and cuisines fields carried embedded commas, quotes, and newlines that broke the CSV parser.

I stopped fighting the tool. The same file loaded into PostgreSQL with zero data loss in seconds. The trick was to load loose — every column as VARCHAR — so dirty values like '--', '₹300', and 'Too Few Ratings' couldn't reject the import. You clean after the data is safely inside.

Choosing the right tool is itself an analytical decision — not a default you fall into.

From the raw staging table, a single CREATE TABLE AS SELECT did the heavy lifting — stripping the rupee symbol and FOR TWO text out of cost, casting ratings to numeric, and converting '--' into proper NULLs alongside a boolean has_rating flag that records why a value is missing.

-- strip '₹' and 'FOR TWO' → integer; '--' rating → NULL
CASE WHEN cost_for_two_string IS NULL THEN NULL
     ELSE CAST(REGEXP_REPLACE(
            REGEXP_REPLACE(cost_for_two_string,'₹',''),
            'FOR TWO','') AS INTEGER) END AS cost_for_two,

CASE WHEN avg_rating = '--' THEN NULL
     ELSE avg_rating::NUMERIC(3,1) END AS avg_rating

Then I bucketed the continuous columns into reporting tiers — rating, cost, delivery speed, review volume — using ordered CASE WHEN logic. Those tiers are what make the dashboard slice-able later.

04 — THE BUG WORTH TELLING

How "North Indian" became two cuisines

The cuisines column was a single string like ['North Indian' 'Chinese' 'South Indian'] — a multi-valued attribute crammed into one cell. To analyse cuisines properly I had to explode it: one restaurant–cuisine pair per row, a classic many-to-many bridge table in first normal form.

My first attempt split on every space. The result was nonsense — "North Indian" shredded into "North" and "Indian", inflating cuisine counts and corrupting every downstream group-by:

-- BROKEN: split on space → multi-word names destroyed
97000  "North"
97000  "Indian"
72350  "South"
72350  "Indian"   -- should have been "South Indian"

The fix was to change the delimiter. Instead of splitting on a space, I split on quote-space-quote — the actual boundary between two quoted items — so multi-word names stay whole:

-- CORRECT: REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE on ' ' (quote-space-quote)
SELECT id AS restaurant_id, TRIM(BOTH '''' FROM cuisine) AS cuisine
FROM (
  SELECT id, REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE(
      SUBSTRING(cuisines_raw FROM 2 FOR LENGTH(cuisines_raw)-2),
      ''' ''') AS cuisine
  FROM restaurants_clean WHERE has_cuisine_data) exploded;

That single delimiter change turned a corrupt table into a clean one: 23,652 restaurant–cuisine relations across 601 distinct cuisines. (My code comments had guessed ~200–300 cuisines — the real number was double, a good reminder to verify guesses against output.)

Finding 1 — Supply is lopsided

Kolkata (1,347) and Mumbai (1,278) anchor the network; Delhi (613) and Surat (513) are thin. Delhi sitting this low is almost certainly a scraping limitation worth flagging — but the maturity gradient across cities is real.

Finding 2 — The operations red flag

Ratings barely move across cities — everyone clusters between 4.01 and 4.18. Quality is not a differentiator. Delivery time is. Kolkata takes ~68 minutes against a 45–59 minute band everywhere else — and it's the largest market. The worst experience sits on top of the biggest restaurant base.

Finding 3 — Price doesn't buy a good rating

This is where Python earned its place. Across all 8,691 restaurants, cost and rating correlate at only r = 0.137 — statistically significant purely because the sample is huge, but practically near-zero. Delivery speed and rating sit at r = –0.045: essentially no relationship at all. Veg restaurants rate marginally higher than non-veg (4.16 vs 4.09, p < 0.0001) but with a Cohen's d of 0.20 — a real-but-negligible gap you shouldn't overclaim.

The discipline that matters A large sample makes almost anything "significant." Reporting effect size next to the p-value — and saying out loud that d = 0.20 is too small to act on — is what separates honest analysis from data theatre.

Finding 4 — The cuisine opportunity is in the middle

The richest insight: what's common is not what's expensive. Mapping each cuisine's average price against how many restaurants serve it splits the market into three clean zones.

  • Premium & rare — Japanese (₹1,162), European, Mediterranean. High margin, but only 37–64 restaurants each. Niche.
  • Cheap & everywhere — North Indian, Chinese, Biryani, Fast Food. The volume backbone; thin per-order value.
  • Accessible-upscale — Italian & Continental price above the median (~₹510–540) and are widely served (600–700 places). The profitable middle — the white space.

06 — THE DASHBOARD

Everything above, in 30 seconds

Findings buried in a notebook help no one. The final deliverable is a two-page Power BI report — an Executive view a VP reads at a glance, and an Analyst Deep Dive with the cuisine-economics scatter, the full city scorecard, and the statistical findings. Every visual is titled as a takeaway, not a label, and slicers (city, veg, cost tier, cuisine) cross-filter the whole canvas live.

Behind it sits the Analyst Deep Dive — same data model, more depth. The cuisine scatter splits the market into price zones, the city scorecard carries a % unrated column the exec page hides, and the findings panel states the statistical takeaways in plain language.

✶ ✶ ✶
07 — SO WHAT

From findings to a decision

Findings only become a "business problem solved" once they turn into actions. Three recommendations close the brief:

01

Fix Kolkata delivery operations first

It's the largest market by supply yet the worst delivery experience at ~68 min. Prioritising delivery-partner density there protects the biggest restaurant base — the highest-leverage operational move on the board.

02

Defend the affordable core, test accessible-premium

The market is firmly mid-budget. Hold that base, but trial Italian/Continental "accessible-upscale" cuisines in saturated metros — they price above median without the rarity of true luxury.

03

Don't compete on quality — it's already uniform

Ratings are flat (4.0–4.2) everywhere and price barely predicts them. Speed and price are the real levers, not chasing higher restaurant ratings that don't differentiate cities.

08 — CRAFT NOTES

What I'd do next

Good analysis names its own gaps. Three I'd close with more time:

  • Investigate the delivery_time units — the distribution skews almost entirely Slow/Very Slow with a single "Very Fast" outlier, which hints the field may not be plain minutes.
  • Handle the cost-for-two = 0 values surfaced in validation — clearly missing rather than free meals.
  • Standardise overlapping cuisine labels (Indian vs North Indian vs South Indian) and add formal primary-key / foreign-key constraints between the two tables.
Why the two-table model matters restaurants_clean is one row per restaurant — the fact table. restaurant_cuisines is the bridge resolving the many-to-many between restaurants and cuisines. That normalisation is what lets the dashboard filter by cuisine and group cleanly, instead of string-parsing on every query — the part most beginner projects skip.
END
